title: Vuelta a Espana: Tadej Pogacar abandons after crashing during stage eight
description: Race leader Tadej Pogacar has abandoned the Vuelta a Espana after crashing during stage eight.The world champion, who was looking to complete a full s
body: Race leader Tadej Pogacar has abandoned the Vuelta a Espana after crashing during stage eight.The world champion, who was looking to complete a full set of Grand Tour victories, crashed with about 33km to go.Pogacar, 27, was riding in the midst of the peloton when he came off his bike, hurting his left shoulder and cutting the left side of his face.The Slovenian appeared to try to get back on his bike before sitting back down again.He then walked unaided into an ambulance. It is the first time he has abandoned a Grand Tour.The overwhelming favourite to win the three-week long race had started the stage three minutes and 50 seconds clear of Spaniard Enric Mas in second place.In what was a chaotic race, another crash occurred in the finishing straight as France's Bryan Coquard claimed his first stage win in a Grand Tour.The 34-year-old edged Lidl-Trek rider Mads Pedersen in a photo finish."I think it has been 13 years, it has been a lot of work and I have finished second a lot of times," Coquard told TNT Sports."I have not been in good positions in the first two sprints, I know I have good legs. Maybe I climb better now, I am fast again."Movistar rider Mas now leads the general classification by one minute and 11 seconds from Decathlon CMA CGM rider Felix Gall.He is the first Spaniard to lead the Vuelta since Jesus Herrada in 2018 but a sombre Mas opted not to wear the red jersey when presented with it on the podium, instead holding it in front of him."It's a real shame," Mas said about Pogacar. "I hope he gets better quickly. We've still got a few races left and I hope he'll be in good shape for them."Six-time Grand Tour winner Pogacar was on course to win all three of the sport's biggest stage races, having already won five Tours de France and a Giro d'Italia.Having become the joint most successful Tour de France champion of all time last month, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider is aiming to become the ninth rider to win all three Grand Tours.Pogacar has also won almost all of the sport's biggest races. In addition to his multiple stage race victories, the two-time road world champion has won 13 one-day monument races, including the Tour of Flanders (three times), Milan-San Remo (once), Il Lombardia (five times) and Liege-Bastogne-Liege (four times).In 2025, he recorded his best finish of second in the other monument - Paris-Roubaix.Pogacar was going to win the Vuelta a Espana by a country mile.Many observers believed his margin of victory could be more than 10 minutes given this much-loved three-week slog typically contains a slightly lower calibre of lead rider.Pogacar was here to further cement his dominance among current riders by becoming only the ninth man to win all three Grand Tours (Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a Espana).He rarely comes to grief on the road; such is his deft bike handling, he never seems to have to wrestle with the handlebars or ever wobble his way down a descent.But this shocking end to Pogacar's Vuelta demonstrates that no-one is invincible.Pogacar won't be entirely devastated - there is plenty of career time for him have another stab at this race. But it is unclear at this stage whether he will be able to defend his coveted rainbow world champion's jersey, given the Road World Championships take place in Canada next month.Vuelta audiences spiked because of the presence of the world's greatest rider for a week, but now there is a real race for the red jersey. At least six previously well-beaten riders suddenly have a shot at glory.

schema.headline: Vuelta a Espana: Tadej Pogacar abandons after crashing during stage eight

title: England vs Pakistan: Michael Vaughan backs Dan Lawrence for run as all-rounder
description: Lawrence, 29, was recalled after an international absence of almost two years, having averaged 26.84 across 14 previous Tests including a stint as a m
body: Lawrence, 29, was recalled after an international absence of almost two years, having averaged 26.84 across 14 previous Tests including a stint as a makeshift opener.By picking him, England prioritised having four pace bowling options over a frontline spinner, with Lawrence backed to provided the overs of slow bowling if needed. He has only bowled one over in the series so far with pace bowlers dominant. On Saturday Lawrence made his mark by coming to the crease at 83-4 and steering England to 177-7 in their second innings when rain brought an early close.The right-hander, whose best Test score remains 91, countered excessive seam movement and uneven bounce by showing attacking intent, hitting six fours and two sixes."He seems to read the game," Vaughan said. "It was the right way to play at that moment. "He has a quirky technique that has worked for him and is very confident. He knows his scoring areas. "He is clearly a better player than when he played for England last time."England's current balance - with Lawrence picked over a frontline spinner - appears suited to home conditions, and could also work in South Africa and Australia where England play this winter. While stronger spin options would likely be needed for the tour of Bangladesh in the new year, the success of England's pace quartet of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue has lessened the need for a spinner in home conditions and, in turn, helped Lawrence's cause.Key selection decisions are still looming, however, with Jacob Bethell currently out of the series because of a knee injury.Bethell, who also bowls part-time spin, could replace Lawrence, or regain his place from Jordan Cox, who has impressed with two fifties while filling in for Bethell at number three.Other options include pushing Cox or Bethell up to open in place of Emilio Gay - Cox opened early in his career in county cricket and Bethell is England's current 50-over opener - and moving Cox down the order to replace Jamie Smith as wicketkeeper.Smith scored an impressive 61 in England's first innings and has improved his glovework after a poor showing in the Ashes."It's pointless looking to the future because it hasn't happened yet," Lawrence said. "I'm just trying to contribute every Test I can and give a good showing of myself."Thankfully, so far, I think I have done."Obviously thoughts creep into your head and I'm desperate, along with all the other boys, to establish myself in an England shirt, which is something I haven't quite done in my career so far."It's just about trying to take every opportunity you get and really enjoy the occasion instead of feeling nervous about the occasion. Just have fun, play the cricket that's got me here this summer."

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: Michael Vaughan backs Dan Lawrence for run as all-rounder

title: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university
description: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to mo
body: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to more students than they realise, and everyone should be taking full advantage."The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Scholarships such as Roehampton's can reduce student debt and provide additional financial support.Thomas Cole, an esports player nicknamed Pac who specialises in the racing game Trackmania, said universities offering unique scholarships, including esports, encourages students academically by reducing the level of financial stress they might face.  "Uni students being paid to play a game alongside doing their studies, it's definitely cracking. If I had gone to uni, I would have loved that," he says."If it doesn't let the academic side suffer, then I think being offered something like that really spurs on people to be better in gaming," he says.Tom Allingham, student money expert from the Save the Student personal finance site, regularly advises incoming first years to seek out scholarships and learn more about what their university offers. "Unfortunately, I don't think there is enough awareness on scholarships," he said. "There is a lot of funding that goes unclaimed because students don't know that they're eligible for it," he added.Save the Student helps share various scholarships and bursaries on their website. "What we try to get across is you can get extra funding for so many different reasons."

schema.headline: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university

title: Royal Navy warships and helicopter track Russian vessels in three-day operation
description: Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North
body: Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North Sea and English Channel.HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels last week, while a Merlin helicopter provided surveillance from the sky."Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys," Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said.It comes as data shows Royal Navy activity to monitor Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.During the August operation, the Royal Navy warships including a Type 45 destroyer and a Type 23 frigate, tracked Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko as it escorted sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta south through the North Sea and into the English Channel. The Royal Navy said Russia was "forced" to respond with "costly military resources" including the frigate Neustrashimy.A statement said a Nato ally then took over monitoring off the coast of France, without specifying the country.The operation comes after Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in June.Marines joined by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers, with the support of the RAF, intercepted and boarded the Smyrtos in a six-hour operation - the first of its kind by UK armed forces.NCA officers arrested an Indian national, 38, on suspicion of sanctions offences under the Russia Regulations and he was taken into custody.

schema.headline: Royal Navy warships and helicopter track Russian vessels in three-day operation

title: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say
description: As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming fr
body: As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month.What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen.Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues.It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary.Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future."I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News."The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria."The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales."People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts."Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries."By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around."Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life."It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts:PandemicsSevere weather and environmental alerts such as flood riskCounter-terrorismBomb dispersal evacuationMajor hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005WildfiresCoal tip landslidesWhen building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children.The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app.It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks.Another one of those involved in creating the alert system, Nick Corney, thinks the government "missed a trick" with the wildfire alert by sending it nationally rather than targeted at specific postcodes with the highest risk.Corney, who worked in the Cabinet Office between 2018 and 2021 and says he was in weekly and then daily meetings about designing alerts, wants a "thorough review".He says this would look at making future alert wording more specific, such as explaining the threat to life with a link to a webpage. "An extra level of consideration needs to be put in place" for national alert versus a local one, he adds."You've really got to take yourself out of the Cobra room," he says."There's a level of scaring the public that needs to be taken into consideration."

schema.headline: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say

title: Alexander Isak: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola must get best out of striker
description: During Liverpool's negotiations with Paris St-Germain for Bradley Barcola, the Anfield hierarchy were determined not to pay more than the club-record
body: During Liverpool's negotiations with Paris St-Germain for Bradley Barcola, the Anfield hierarchy were determined not to pay more than the club-record £125m they spent on Alexander Isak last summer.When the £123m deal for Barcola is completed over the coming days, the France winger will become the 10th £100m player in Premier League history.None have cost more than Isak, so the expectation on the former Newcastle striker is understandable, to say the least.Isak scored 44 Premier League goals in his last two seasons at Newcastle, but in an injury-plagued first campaign at Anfield the 26-year-old found the back of the net just three times in 14 top-flight appearances.For Andoni Iraola, who has drawn his first two games as Liverpool manager, a major part of success at Anfield will be the ability to get the best out of Isak, who - despite scoring - was largely ineffective in their 2-2 draw against Nottingham Forest on Saturday.Unlike last summer, Isak has looked sharp in pre-season after some impressive displays for Sweden at the World Cup, but struggled on his return to Tyneside last weekend.For 45 minutes against Forest on Saturday, those struggles continued with just six touches, one accurate pass and zero shots. "It is clear that Liverpool haven't worked out how to play with Alexander Isak yet," said ex-England goalkeeper Joe Hart, who is a pundit on Saturday's Match of the Day."At Newcastle everything flowed through him. That was down to a trust thing that they had built up over time - their midfield knew exactly where he was and they didn't even need to look up as he'd be there waiting."At Liverpool that trust just isn't there at the moment - no-one is feeling it and he isn't that central point, which is leading to him looking lost and isolated."It would have been intriguing to be a fly on the wall in the directors' box at Anfield. Iraola's first home Premier League game was watched by incoming Liverpool vice-chairman Amit Bhatia, principal owner John Henry, and sporting director Richard Hughes, who was integral in getting the deal for Isak done last summer. Thankfully for them - and Iraola - Isak got Liverpool on level terms after the break. He managed just seven more touches in the second half but centre-forwards deal in goals and the Swede timed his run perfectly to meet Cody Gakpo's delivery for his first goal of the season. His smile after told a story in itself."That's the job ultimately as a striker [to score goals]. I am very happy to score the first one and hopefully it just keeps coming," Isak told TNT Sports.Former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard described the goal as "big" - for both the striker's confidence and the team's.But, in Hart's opinion, Iraola still has a major conundrum."Andoni Iraola has some big decisions to make," said Hart. "Does he base his team round him [Isak] or does he try to find a different solution within his squad? In my opinion he's got to commit to what the club have done by investing so heavily in Isak."There's no point signing these players if you aren't going to use them properly and play to their strengths. There's no doubting Isak's quality - they are just at a bit of a crossroads at the moment."During Isak's struggles last season, the belief inside the club was that he was a long-term signing and judgement would be reserved for once he was fully fit.Only Erling Haaland, Mohamed Salah and Ollie Watkins have scored more Premier League goals since Isak's first season in England and, with Salah now out of the picture, the onus is on Isak to deliver - particularly with Hugo Ekitike out injured.Liverpool's first two games of the season have finished 2-2 despite Iraola's side enjoying 60% of possession against Newcastle last week and 70% against Forest.In both games, they have found themselves trailing and are yet to be ahead in the Premier League this season.That has inevitably made things trickier for Isak, who was such a force in a counter-attacking Newcastle side. Against low blocks, the proposition is different.It is also symptomatic of a wider issue Iraola faces.Last season, his Bournemouth side won just four of the 19 Premier League games in which they had the majority of possession. They won nine of the other 19.The Cherries, who were known for their counter-pressing style and effectiveness in transition, also failed to win a game in which they had more than 58.8% possession.In essence, his side were more successful when they had less of the ball - something that will rarely happen now he is at Anfield."As an attacking force it isn't flowing for Liverpool," said Hart. "With the physical nature of the Premier League and with them not 100% sure on what they are doing at the moment, teams are stomping all over them."It's going to take a whole lot of work from Iraola and his staff on the training pitch, but he is a top coach and they have top players."Asked about whether he sets targets for the season, Isak said: "Not really. I think every striker wants to score [in] every game he plays. Obviously that's difficult but [we take] each game at a time."That is one way to look at it, and this was certainly an improvement on his showing against Newcastle, but deep down Isak will know he can - and must - do better.

schema.headline: Alexander Isak: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola must get best out of striker

title: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand: Springboks level 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series
description: 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second TestSouth Africa (24) 33Tries: Kriel, De Allende, Kolisi Cons: Kolbe 3 Pens: Kolbe 4New Zealand (14) 26Trie
body: 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second TestSouth Africa (24) 33Tries: Kriel, De Allende, Kolisi Cons: Kolbe 3 Pens: Kolbe 4New Zealand (14) 26Tries: Roigard, McKenzie, Carter, Savea Cons: Love 3World champions South Africa delivered a powerful first-half performance as they edged past New Zealand and levelled 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1 with two Tests to play.The All Blacks travelled to Cape Town knowing a win would write them into the history books as the first New Zealand team to win back-to-back Tests in South Africa since the 'Incomparables' of 1996.But South Africa dominated the basics and showed a more clinical edge this week, even though the lively All Blacks again outscored them on the try count by four to three.New Zealand's fightback ultimately came too late, captain Ardie Savea barging over on 77 minutes to get the game within a score, but on the All Blacks' final attack Boks replacement Cameron Hanekom won a superb turnover that settled the nervy closing stages.As he did last week, Springboks wing Cheslin Kolbe took on the kicking duties over fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, notching up 18 points in a player-of-the-match performance.The first series in 30 years between these two mighty rugby nations is shaping into an epic, with the third Test back at altitude in Soweto, Johannesburg next Saturday.Despite producing a famous rearguard effort in the first-Test victory at Ellis Park, New Zealand boss Dave Rennie warned in the week his side would need to "go deeper" to cope with the inevitable Springbok backlash.That South African onslaught came from the off.Hooker Deon Fourie, at nearly 40 the oldest Springbok in history, found his target in the line-out, the South African maul powered into the 22, and lightning fast ball led to centre Jesse Kriel crashing over.Kolbe added the extras as the world champions made the dream start.But despite the fast start from the hosts, New Zealand grew into the contest, with referee Angus Gardner, himself a late call-up in place of Nika Amashukeli, presiding over a fast and fluent game.Damian McKenzie made a clean break which almost put in Will Jordan, and while the Boks killed the ball from the ensuing breakdown, Eben Etzebeth got up to spoil New Zealand's five-metre line-out.Despite their set-piece issues, the All Blacks came again. Intricate handling freed Jordan, who used his pace and strength to escape down the right and link with the outstanding Cam Roigard. Ruben Love levelled the scores from bang in front.That score lit a fire in the Springboks, with Kolbe kicking a penalty and Damian de Allende barrelling over after another imposing maul as South Africa showed far more ruthlessness compared to a week ago.With the Springboks dominating in the basics, the crowd in Cape Town smelt blood as the lead stretched to 17-7.But with ball in hand, Rennie's crop are reminiscent of the great All Blacks side of old. Savea burst forward from a line-out, and perfect passing gave McKenzie a walk-in.At 17-14 edging towards half-time the contest was in the balance, before a match-defining sequence just before the interval.Kolbe forced a five-metre scrum, before which Erasmus brought on two of his strongest scrummagers in Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche, who immediately won a penalty.From there, another scrum, another penalty advantage, and with the All Blacks back-pedalling captain Siya Kolisi crashed over for South Africa's third try and a 10-point lead after a pulsating first 40.New Zealand needed to score first in the second half, and they didn't, losing the ball when in Bok territory and then giving away a soft penalty which Kolbe kicked.The All Blacks were on the ropes, Marx won a breakdown penalty, and Kolbe stretched the lead to 16 points with half an hour to go.With the second half lacking the fireworks of the first, the All Blacks backs – led by Roigard - desperately tried to drag New Zealand back into the match.After another McKenzie break led to nothing, some more beautiful handling resulted in Leroy Carter scampering into the left corner, a fabulous finish.More excellent attacking play released Jordan down the right, and the recycled ball found skipper Savea, who crashed over to cut the gap to seven points with two minutes remaining.But the Springboks held on, despite lock Lood de Jager being sent to the sin-bin for a high tackle.Fittingly, it was a breakdown penalty that settled the game, with Hanekom winning the crucial turnover in an area South Africa dominated.The All Blacks' impressive win in the first Test had temporarily shot them above South Africa in the world rankings, something Erasmus urged his side to rectify.That they did, and with normal service resumed in the eyes of the Springboks supporters, South Africa travel back to the Highveld with the momentum.But the All Blacks have played some wonderful rugby in the first two Tests, and will still believe they can join the legends of 1996.The eyes of the rugby world now turn to Soweto.South Africa: Willemse; Kolbe, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi (capt), Du Toit, WieseReplacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, Du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, LibbokNew Zealand: McKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea, J Barrett, Carter; Love, Roigard; Bower, Taylor, Lomax, Holland, Vaa'i, Parker, Jacobson, Savea (capt)Replacements: Aumua, Numia, Newell, Tuipulotu, Lakai, Preston, Lienert-Brown, Moorby

schema.headline: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand: Springboks level 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series

title: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil
description: The US has struck a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, Donald Trump announced.The US president wr
body: The US has struck a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, Donald Trump announced.The US president wrote that the agreement would more than double American oil reserves and "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans".Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez hailed the deal as one that would help her nation's economic revival.But some analysts have reacted with scepticism, including questioning whether the deal would address long-running obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela's oil industry.Trump has recently been under domestic pressure to tame petrol prices, which have spiked due to the Iran war.He vowed to tap into Venezuela's reserves, the world's largest, after the US captured its then-President Nicolás Maduro in January, ostensibly to stand trial on drug charges in New York.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the oil deal "a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people". Few details were released."For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100bn (£74bn) in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy," he said.Trump said Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had reached the agreement with Venezuela's leadership "through a partnership with private business".He did not elaborate on the partnership or describe possible commitments and terms for the US in the deal, but he claimed the agreement was reached "at no cost to the American Taxpayer".Under the deal the US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's US partner CBS News. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that US energy firms Chevron and Halliburton were nearing deals to invest billions in overhauling the infrastructure in Venezuela's oil fields, many of which have not been developed.David Goldwyn, president of energy consultancy Goldwyn Global Strategies, said there was "no precedent" for the US government entering into a lease to operate Venezuelan oil fields.It's not clear if such a move would violate Venezuela's constitution or its hydrocarbons law, he told the Reuters news agency."It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale," he added, citing Venezuela's political uncertainty, weak power grid, and limited export capacity. Venezuela's interim president said in a statement that the agreement would have "a significant impact on our nation's revival".The deal calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100bn and more than $209bn in taxes" for Venezuela, Rodríguez said."These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernisation of our industry, but also to our country's economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater balance in international markets," she said.Oil, gas and mineral lawyer Alexander Kuiper told the BBC the deal could be "very significant" but expressed some caution."This is definitely a headline to help with oil prices," he said, but added: "What we don't know, is whether or not those reserves turn into actual investment, and how long that investment takes to produce results."Asked how it would affect oil prices in practice, Kuiper said: "There isn't a switch that you can flip - contracts and agreements have to be put in place... this could take a long time, but it's an important first step."Delcy Rodríguez - Maduro's former vice-president, who the US backed following his capture - gave the venture a 100-year concession to operate in the oil fields, the unnamed US official told CBS.Trump gave few specifics of the highly unusual agreement, which apparently grants the US direct governance over a foreign country's sovereign national resources.The deal would also appear to be wider in scope than the US-led Coalition Provisional Authority's control over Iraq's oil revenues after Saddam Hussein was ousted in an American-led invasion in 2003.But it is unclear whether the Venezuela agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in the South American nation. The official text of the agreement between Washington and Caracas has not been published.Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world - an estimated 303 billion barrels. However, production has plummeted since its peak in the late 1990s, in part due to a tightening of controls over its state-run oil firm and US sanctions targeting its main economic lifeline.Hours after US special forces captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a raid on the Venezuelan capital, Trump said the US would indefinitely control the sale of the country's oil.He has also claimed the rights to Venezuela's oil after saying that the country had in the past "unilaterally seized and sold American oil, American assets and American platforms, costing us billions and billions of dollars".His framing of the deal as part of efforts to drive down domestic petrol prices comes as the global price of oil has jumped up significantly as supply via the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf has effectively been stymied - spurring discontent ahead of the US midterm elections in November.However, Venezuela's oil reserves are made up of so-called "heavy, sour" oil, which is harder to refine and used for making diesel and asphalt, while the US typically produces "light, sweet" oil useful for making petrol.Trump has asked US oil firms to invest at least $100bn (£75bn) to restore the country's oil industry.

schema.headline: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil

title: Nepal flood devastation revealed in satellite imagery
description: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.Satellite images also show the formation of a barrie
body: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

schema.headline: Nepal flood devastation revealed in satellite imagery

title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
description: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launc
body: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled. Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it. It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents. The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long. Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

schema.headline: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there

title: How Victorian Eastbourne realised it needed public loos
description: How a seaside town realised it needed public loosImage source, Kevin GordonImage caption, The Queens Hotel, boasting 60 rooms, was one of the faciliti
body: How a seaside town realised it needed public loosImage source, Kevin GordonImage caption, The Queens Hotel, boasting 60 rooms, was one of the facilities without a toiletBySimon FurberReporting fromin Eastbourne and Cash MurphySouth EastEastbourne has a fascinating history with one of life's most basic amenities: the toilet.In the Victorian era, as the town grew from a small settlement into one of Britain's most fashionable seaside resorts, thousands of tourists arrived by train each year.But the number of toilets did not match the number of visitors and a popular boat race in 1870 laid bare the lack of facilities."It's said that over 1,000 people used a small stable near the pier to go the toilet," historian Kevin Gordon told Secret Sussex.Figure caption, Eastbourne's battle with convenience"I'm not even sure if it was plumbed in; this obviously made the council realise that they needed to do something about this problem," Gordon explained. He said that one of the first toilets was built at the Wish Tower slopes close to the seafront, on land that was then owned by the military.While that toilet, which was notably only for men, was put in place in 1873, the first sign for it was not erected until 17 years later.A growing interest in building public toilets put Trinity Trees - a street in the centre of Eastbourne that eventually became another site for an early public toilet - at the centre of a debate. Plans to construct facilities were not universally embraced."[Some] people didn't want a toilet there at all. The Duke of Devonshire said he didn't want any toilets, public toilets, on his land because he called them 'violations of public decency'," said Gordon. Image source, Kevin GordonImage caption, Gentleman's toilets were hidden in the bushes near the Wish Tower, pictured in the late 1800sEven when toilets were built, they weren't for everyone. Gordon said the council didn't introduce the first public ladies' toilets until 1900. Plans had previously been turned down by the council, which remember, was male led, he said. According to Gordon, the town's soaring popularity prompted the council to finally take action.He said: "Thousands of people were coming down here by train, and I don't think the council initially realised that they needed the ordinary things that we all want."The refurbished toilets at Eastbourne Pier, the bandstand, Holywell and Beachy Head are now £1 to use.Secret SussexExplore more fascinating stories from SussexListen and subscribe for the latest episode of Secret Sussex

title: Box breathing: Inside the 'most powerful hack' to control stress
description: How one of the 'most powerful hacks' to control stress actually worksImage source, @breathpodImage caption, Stuart Sandeman says breathwork originates
body: How one of the 'most powerful hacks' to control stress actually worksImage source, @breathpodImage caption, Stuart Sandeman says breathwork originates from traditional practices like yogaByGeorge SandemanPowerless to help after catastrophic earthquakes struck her hometown of La Guaira in Venezuela two months ago, Maria Medina struggled to sleep.She was more than 1,500 miles away in Florida, USA - where she has lived for the last 15 years - and was racked with worry for family and friends.Box breathing helped her combat sleepless nights."In moments where I feel that there isn't much that I can do, like lying in bed at night and staring at the ceiling... I know it's going to help me," she says.The 31-year-old first came across box breathing in 2020. She was studying for a master's degree while working full-time and the stress of doing both became too much once the Covid pandemic hit. She sought help from a therapist who showed her how to box breathe.Image source, @mariadelmar.msImage caption, Maria Medina uses box breathing when she has trouble sleepingThe technique consists of inhaling for four seconds, holding your breath for four seconds, exhaling for four seconds and then holding for another four seconds before inhaling again and restarting the cycle, says breathwork coach Stuart Sandeman."Those seconds can be all sorts of lengths, but they must all remain the same," he explains. This equal four-step pattern is where the technique derives its name.Stuart says box breathing is best used before you do something stressful or an event that might cause you to feel anxious, like an exam or presentation.There's no set length of time to do it for. Some people feel the positive effects after just a few minutes; others prefer to do it for as long as 15.This Instagram post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on InstagramThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.Skip instagram postAllow Instagram content?This article contains content provided by Instagram.  We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies.  You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.Breathwork originated from traditional practices like yoga and has been used in other fields like martial arts for centuries, says Stuart. But box breathing has become popular in modern times because it can "both focus the mind and allow us to balance our nervous system".He adds: "Famously, the US Navy Seals are box breathers. They use it before going into a hostile situation."Stuart has also taught breathwork to the England football team.For Maria, 31, who works as a programme manager for a tech company in the US, she does it before she goes to bed, or when trying to get back to sleep after waking up in the night.The last hold is most importantA recent study, external from North America looking at the effectiveness of box breathing found it could prevent large increases in heart rate and other stress markers in the body among people facing high-pressure situations.The study, published in the journal Comprehensive Psychoneuroendocrinology in June, was undertaken by academics at Texas State University and the University of Toronto Mississauga. Dr Helen Garr, a GP who treats doctors and nurses suffering mental health difficulties, says: "I recommend box breathing to lots of my patients because it is one of the most powerful evidence-based hacks that we have to take control of our stress response and our nervous system."She says the last step of box breathing, where you hold after you exhale, is what causes the greatest change physiologically."What is happening inside our bodies during the final hold is that we are retaining carbon dioxide (CO2) and when our brain detects the increased levels of CO2, it feels panic. We feel that urge to breathe."That final hold trains us to better cope with higher levels of CO2 in our system and reduce that feeling of stress, she says. People breathe differently when they're stressed, which leads to changes in their body's CO2 levels.Image source, NHS Practitioner HealthImage caption, Dr Helen Garr recommends box breathing to the doctors and nurses she treats"Box breathing trains us to get used to variations in carbon dioxide in the blood and in the brain and helps overcome feelings of panic," she explains.Unlike Maria, Brittany Lamm doesn't box breathe before she goes to sleep but does so after waking up."I do it every morning," the 28-year-old tells me from her home in California. "I actually did it just before you called me."She found out about box breathing online a few years ago when she was going through a difficult time in her personal life and was looking for ways to cope with the stress of it.Many people who use box breathing, from former soldiers to lifestyle influencers, share tips on how others can use it in their lives. Some also post animated guides for people to follow along with."If you wake up feeling anxious, it's a really great tool to help get you back into your body and out of your head," says Brittany.It helps her feel a sense of control over her thoughts and emotions instead of letting them dictate her day.She found it so effective that she learnt about other breathing techniques and incorporates them into her work as a life coach. She did a degree in psychology and is training to be a licensed therapist.Image source, @mindful.by.bImage caption, Brittany uses box breathing at the beginning of meetings with her clients"I do it with my clients when we start our calls,  so that they feel calmer than when they arrived."If we're talking about [emotionally] heavy topics, like what's going on in their relationship, it makes it a little bit easier for them."She appreciates that some people might be sceptical about the difference breathing techniques actually make to stressful situations but urges people to try them."Breathwork isn't a one-size-fits-all. There's so many different types for whatever you might be feeling or going through."She adds: "Nine out of 10 people that I work with say they really do feel so much better afterwards."Maria feels similarly and has recommended box breathing to many friends and colleagues who have gone through stressful periods.Fortunately for her, none of her immediate family died in the Venezuela earthquakes which are estimated to have killed at least 6,300 people."But my best friend lost her home and I know people who lost family and friends."Sleepless nights still afflict Maria occasionally but box breathing is something she knows can help her deal with periods that might feel overwhelming."I think that sometimes we forget to breathe, like really intentionally breathe, and we underestimate the powers that it might bring to our body and mind."

title: Football fans tribute to crash death Cleveland Police officers
description: Earlier this week 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash bringing the total number of arrests to 24.The occupants
body: Earlier this week 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash bringing the total number of arrests to 24.The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.Speaking earlier on Radio 4's Today programme, Middlesbrough mayor Chris Cooke said Cleveland Police was doing "extremely well" despite a lack of funding that "they absolutely need"."They are a police force that has been the hardest hit. "They've had over 10 per cent reduction in FTE (full-time equivalent) of police officers, while other places have seen over 20 per cent increase, and that isn't fair," he said.Cooke added police funding should "follow need"."It cannot just be based on population sizes as it currently is, because that serves no one well," he said.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.

title: Tottenham Hotspur v Newcastle: How the players rated
description: Antonin Kinsky: Unlike his countryman, Lukas Hornicek, the Spurs goalkeeper had nothing to do in the first half but could only watch on as Elanga's sh
body: Antonin Kinsky: Unlike his countryman, Lukas Hornicek, the Spurs goalkeeper had nothing to do in the first half but could only watch on as Elanga's shot went in off the post after the break before Wissa's improvised effort made it 2-0. 5Archie Gray: Can never fault his effort but is he at his very best at right-back? 5Micky van de Ven: The captain's first start of the season. Picked up a needless early booking, but went on to make a crucial sliding challenge to deny Wissa inside the box. 6Jan Paul van Hecke: Got back to make a block to deny Willock. Comfort in possession allowed Spurs to bypass Newcastle press. Went close with header. 6Andy Robertson: Carried a threat going forward in the first half but could not prevent Dedic winning a header to set up Elanga's goal. 5Rodrigo Bentancur: Work often goes unseen. Broke up play and won ball back on a number of occasions. 5Sandro Tonali: A shaky start as he came up against his former club for the first time. Clearly still building up fitness. At fault in build up to both goals. Ironically cheered by away fans as he came off. 4Mateus Fernandes: First Premier League start for club. Always looked to be positive and deliveries from corners caused one or two problems in first half. 5Pedro Porro: The World Cup winner played further forward on the right wing and had a couple of openings, seeing a shot blocked by Hall and a dipping volley go just over. 5Omar Marmoush: Debutant was quickly parachuted into starting line-up, having tormented Newcastle so many times before with Manchester City. Hit side netting on volley. Smart reverse pass created opening for Robertson. 6Mathys Tel: Saw one stinging effort well-saved, but also frustrated the crowd by giving the ball away. 4Subs:Kudus (on 68, Tel): Welcome return after being sidelined since January with a serious quad injury 5Moore (on 68, Gray): 5Udogie (on 68, Robertson) 5Dominic Solanke (on 75, Tonali): 5Subs not used: Dubravka, Senesi, Gallagher, Bergvall, DaviesLukas Hornicek: Made saves to keep out Tel, Robertson and van Hecke's efforts when Newcastle were under pressure in the first half. His save from van Hecke's header left head coach Matthias Jaissle clenching his fists on the touchline. 7Amar Dedic: Another impressive all-round performance from the summer signing little more than a week-and-a-half into his Newcastle career. Great knock-down header to set up first goal. Tino Livramento faces a real battle to win back his place. 7Malick Thiaw: Captain again in Dan Burn's absence. A proper old-fashioned tussle with Marmoush at times, who kept him on his toes. 6Sven Botman: Had a shaky pre-season but looking more assured. Appears to be benefitting from a run of games with the same back four. 6Lewis Hall: Made a huge last-ditch block inside the box to prevent Porro from getting a shot away in first half. Defensively solid and no penalty fears this time. 7Nico Gonzalez: An impressive debut. Kept composure even after booking. A stunning cross-field ball in the build up to Elanga's goal. 8Lewis Miley: Goes about his work quietly but keeps the ball so well. 7Anthony Elanga: Looks a reborn player full of confidence under Jaissle. Scored his second goal in two games with a smart turn and finish in off the post. His was the name repeatedly sung by the away supporters. 7. Joe Willock: Made an instant impact after coming off the bench against Liverpool, but not as effective as a starter on Saturday. Got one of biggest cheers from Newcastle fans for a meaty challenge on Tonali. 5Harvey Barnes: Fresh from scoring two goals in the midweek win over West Brom in the Carabao Cup, but did not offer same threat this time. Fired one effort way over and failed to pick out a team-mate on one promising breakaway after his cutback went straight into traffic. 5Yoane Wissa: Led the line in injured William Osula's absence and repeatedly dropped deep to help his side. Clever overhead kick sealed the win. 7Subs:Sean Steur (on 71, Gonzalez): Sent in teasing deliver with corner in build up to Wissa's goal. 7Nick Woltemade (on 71, Willock): Header set up Newcastle's second from Steur's corner. 7Subs not used: Jaouen, Schar, Bamba, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey, Shahar
